The Prophet raised his hands to his shoulders or ears when beginning the prayer, before bowing and on rising from it, but not between the prostrations.
Abu Huraira said takbir at every bending and rising, calling his prayer the closest to the Prophet's, and Ali's prayer with takbir reminded Imran of the Prophet's.
Prayer without the Fatiha is not credited; Allah divides it between Himself and His servant verse by verse, and Abu Huraira says it suffices, though reciting more is better.
A man sent back three times to pray again was taught to perform ablution, face the Qibla, say takbir, recite, and bow, prostrate and sit calmly.
The Prophet felt a man reciting behind him was disputing his recitation; Anas never heard the Prophet, Abu Bakr, Umar or Uthman recite Bismillah aloud.
Wa'il saw the Prophet raise his hands, place right over left and prostrate between his palms; he taught the tashahhud like a surah, and Abu Musa relayed following the imam.
The Prophet told people to perform their bowing and prostration well, saying he saw them behind his back as he saw in front.
Worshippers must not lift their eyes to the sky in prayer or wave their hands at the salutation like headstrong horses' tails, but be calm and form rows like angels.
In noon and afternoon prayers the Prophet recited al-Fatiha and a surah in the first two rak'ahs, longer than the last two, as Sa'd told Umar he too did.
In the morning prayer the Prophet recited Surah Qaf, al-Mu'minun and the like, sixty to a hundred verses, prolonging it more than the noon and afternoon prayers.
The Prophet recited Surat al-Tur and the surah Umm al-Fadl last heard from him in the evening prayer, and 'By the Fig' in the night prayer on a journey.
The Prophet's standing, bowing, rising, prostrating and sitting were nearly balanced, and he and Anas paused after bowing and between prostrations so long that people thought they had forgotten.
On rising from bowing the Prophet praised his Lord with praise filling the heavens and earth, saying none can withhold what He gives, and asked to be purified with snow.
The Prophet said only good visions remain of prophethood's glad tidings and forbade reciting the Quran in bowing and prostration, which are for glorifying the Lord and supplication.
The Prophet was commanded to prostrate on seven bones, forehead, hands, knees and feet, and not to fold back hair or clothing; Ibn Abbas undid a man's plaited hair.
In prostration the forearms are not spread like a dog's: palms down, elbows raised, the Prophet's arms so wide his armpits showed; Aisha described his prayer from takbir to taslim.
Ibn Mas'ud bowed with palms between his thighs, but Sa'd said this was later replaced by palms on the knees; Ibn Abbas called a sitting hard on the foot sunnah.
Sitting for the tashahhud, the Prophet placed his hands on his thighs or knees and pointed with his forefinger, and ended the prayer with salutations to the right and left.
Between the opening takbir and the recitation the Prophet silently asked Allah to remove and wash away his sins, but in the second rak'ah he began al-Fatiha without pause.
The Prophet prayed and prostrated on a small mat, his garment touching Maimuna beside him when he prostrated.
After prayer the Prophet turned to the left as well as to the right, and companions liked to stand at his right so his face would turn to them.
The most excellent prayer is the one in which the standing is longest.
